title: Design a rate limiter
question: How would you design a distributed rate limiter?

problem.statement: Design a rate limiter for a public API: each client may make at most 100 requests per minute.
example: Limit by user, API key or IP address
Tell the client when to try again
constraints: 1 million requests per second across many servers
Adds under 2 ms to each request
The limit holds no matter which server a request lands on
If the limiter breaks, the API keeps working
problem.followUp: How do you stop two servers both letting the 101st request through?

steps.caption: What the interviewer is really asking.

plain.asking: Give every client a *fair share* of the API, and politely turn away whatever goes over it, the same way on every server.
points: *Must work:* count requests per client; refuse the extras with a retry time.
*Must be fast:* every single request pays for this check.
*Out of scope:* billing, detecting attackers by behaviour.

steps.caption: Your API is open to everyone. Ana and Raj make a few requests each. Then a *buggy script* starts firing thousands a second.

steps.caption: Put a *rate limiter* at the door. Each client gets a fair share, say 100 requests a minute. Anything extra is turned away right there.

steps.caption: Refused requests get *429 Too Many Requests* and a hint: “try again in 12 seconds”. A well-behaved client waits instead of hammering.

items.label: RATE LIMITER

steps.caption: How does the limiter count? Picture each client holding a *bucket of tokens*. A tap drips new tokens in at a steady rate.
Every request must take *one token* out to get through. Here one goes in, takes a token, and reaches the API. 9 tokens left.
A sudden burst of requests drains the bucket fast. Once it is *empty*, the next request finds no token and is refused.
The tap keeps dripping: one token every 0.6 seconds, so 100 a minute. *Short bursts are allowed, but the average is capped.*

check.question: The bucket holds 10 tokens and gains 1 per second. A client sends 10 requests at once, then an 11th right after. What happens?
options: All 10 pass; the 11th waits for the next token
check.explain: The full bucket pays for the burst of 10. The 11th finds it *empty* and is refused until a token drips back in about a second later.

steps.caption: At scale there are many limiter copies. If each keeps its *own* bucket, a client whose requests land on two copies gets *double* the limit.

items.label: BUGGY SCRIPT
items.note: A client stuck in a retry loop, firing as fast as it can.

items.label: API SERVERS
items.note: The real work: database queries, business logic.

items.label: GATEWAYS
items.note: Many copies of the limiter, behind a load balancer.

steps.caption: Keep the buckets in one fast shared store, *Redis*. Every limiter copy takes tokens from the same bucket, so the limit holds wherever a request lands.

steps.caption: Careful: two limiter copies look at the bucket at the same instant and both see *1 token left*. Both take it. One token, two requests through.

steps.caption: Make “check and take a token” a single *atomic* step inside Redis, a tiny script that can’t be interrupted. The second copy finds the bucket empty.

check.question: Why is “read the tokens, then write tokens − 1” unsafe with many limiter copies?
options: Two copies can read the same value before either writes
check.explain: Between one copy’s read and its write, another copy can read the same value. An *atomic* script closes that gap.

steps.caption: If Redis itself fails, choose: *fail open* (let traffic through, unlimited for a while) or fail closed (refuse everything). Most APIs fail open.

steps.caption: Buckets allow short bursts. If the limit must be *exact* in every 60-second window, a sliding-window log stores each request’s time instead, at more memory.
